extracted.intended_audience: researchers in scientometrics/bibliometrics and NLP practitioners developing/using citation-context/classification methods
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical findings for analyzing citation content and context to identify citation function, polarity, and influence using manual annotation or automated classifiers; includes recommended context sizes, feature sets (linguistic, positional, bibliometric), and evaluation notes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation context window size
rubrics_metrics.description: How large a textual window around a reference anchor should be analyzed (single sentence, sentence before/after, 3 sentences, 4 sentences, etc.) to capture the citation's meaning/function.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Longer contexts generally improve downstream tasks: Halevi & Moed (2013) recommend analyzing the sentence containing the citation plus one sentence before and after; Ritchie et al. (2008) found three-sentence windows outperform one-sentence for IR; Yousif et al. (2018) found four sentences improved classification for purpose/sentiment. Some citation contexts span multiple sentences (22% had two or more sentences in Abu-Jbara et al., 2013). Choose larger windows when discourse continues beyond the citing sentence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manual vs automated data processing tradeoffs
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice between manual annotation (human reading of citation contexts) and automated computational classification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manual annotation yields richer, domain-informed labels but is time-consuming, tedious, and subjective (annotators may lack domain expertise). Automated methods scale but current classification schemes can yield unreliable results; combining manual annotation to build/validate corpora with automated experiments (machine learning) is common. Report inter-annotator subjectivity, dataset size, and limitations when using automated labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation function classifications (Teufel et al. 2006)
rubrics_metrics.description: A four-category scheme for citation function: weak (points to weaknesses), contrast (comparisons/contrasts), positive (positive sentiment), neutral (neutral description).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used with features like cue phrases and citation location; Teufel et al. achieved ≈75% accuracy for function classification and 83% for polarity on their dataset. Consider whether to separate polarity and function or combine them depending on task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation function classifications (Li et al. 2013 annotation scheme)
rubrics_metrics.description: A combined function+polarity labeling where each function is labeled as positive (+), neutral (=), or negative (−). Functions include Based on+, Corroboration+, Discover+, Positive+, Practical+, Significant+, Standard+, Supply+, Contrast=, Co-citation=, Neutral=, Negative-.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Designs like this capture both purpose and sentiment simultaneously. Li et al.'s scheme (91 PubMed papers; n=6355 citation instances) achieved 67% accuracy; class imbalance affected performance—some functions rare. Use balanced corpora or reporting strategies for skewed labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation purpose taxonomy (Jha et al. 2017)
rubrics_metrics.description: A six-category purpose taxonomy for citation contexts: criticizing, comparison, use, substantiating, basis, and natural.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Jha et al. annotated combined purpose and polarity (30 ACL papers, n=3500). They report purpose classification accuracy ≈70.5% and polarity detection accuracy 84.2%. They used features like number of references in context, lone vs multiple references, negation cues, and self-citation. ‘Use’ was most frequent (17.7%).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation polarity (sentiment) — positive/neutral/negative
rubrics_metrics.description: Labeling citation contexts by sentiment/polarity toward the cited work: positive, neutral, or negative.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Polarity alone is informative but combining polarity with function improves understanding and classifier performance (Li et al., Jha et al.). Polarity classifiers have achieved 83–93% accuracy in some studies (Teufel 83%, Hernández-Alvarez et al. 93%). Define clear annotation rules for what constitutes positive/negative (e.g., explicit strengths vs pointing to weaknesses).

rubrics_metrics.name: Citation influence classification (perfunctory vs significant positive vs significant negative)
rubrics_metrics.description: Classify citations by their influence on the citing work: perfunctory (trivial/marginal), significant positive (relevant + positive), significant negative (relevant + negative).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hernández-Alvarez et al. (2017) proposed this three-way influence scheme and reported high accuracies (in their experiment: function 89%, polarity 93%, influence 94%). Influence labels can be derived from combined function+polarity and contextual features; clarify definitions (e.g., perfunctory often correlates with neutral polarity).

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of linguistic pattern features (hedge cues, verbs, cue words)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exploit lexical/linguistic markers in citation contexts—hedge cues (may, likely), verbs (show, use), nouns/prepositions—to infer citation function or paper type.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hedge cues distribute unevenly across sections (Di Marco et al. 2006): more frequent in results/discussion. Verb distributions differ by section (Bertin & Atanassova 2014): e.g., 'show' frequent in introduction/discussion; 'describe' in methods. Use lists of cue phrases and verb-frequency features; beware that multiple cue phrases in one sentence can reduce precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cue-phrase groupings for function detection (Wang et al. 2012)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use curated groups of cue phrases mapped to citation types (e.g., 'extend', 'criticize', 'improve', 'compare') to detect functions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Wang et al. used 48 cue groups (24 for extend, 12 for criticize, 8 for compare, 5 for improve). Their precision varied by type (extend 72%, criticize 60%, improve 33%, compare 29%)—expanding cue lists can increase recall but may introduce ambiguity. Consider combining cue phrases with other features (location, co-citations) to raise precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citance vs citation context distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Distinguish a citance (a single sentence containing one or more references) from broader citation contexts (multiple surrounding sentences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tasks differ: Small et al. used citances to detect discovery and method papers; citances are compact and useful for lexical-based classifiers, while larger contexts may better capture argumentative functions. Choose the unit (citance vs multi-sentence context) based on the target task.

rubrics_metrics.name: Section/location-sensitive features
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for the location of the citation within the paper (introduction, methods, results, discussion) when inferring function or influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Many studies find function and linguistic signals vary by section (hedges more in results/discussion; methods use passive voice; background tends to be active). Features like 'number of different sections referencing a paper' and 'percentage of citances in method sections' are predictive of influence/type (Small 2018; Valenzuela/Zhu/Pride & Knoth).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bibliometric and structural predictors of influence
rubrics_metrics.description: Use non-linguistic features such as total number of times a paper is cited within the citing paper, author overlap (self-citation), number of sections citing the reference, and abstract similarity to predict whether a citation is influential.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies (Valenzuela et al., Zhu et al., Pride & Knoth) consistently find only a small fraction of citations are influential (~10–15%). 'Total number of times a paper is cited in the citing paper' is a strong predictor (single-feature accuracy often modest but improves when combined with section-count and self-citation). Report feature importances and combine features for best results (precision up to 90% reported in some models).

rubrics_metrics.name: Word-combination and auxiliary predictors for paper-type classification
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine lexical cues (e.g., 'using', 'may', 'show', 'not', 'suggest') with non-linguistic variables (consensus, section distribution, age) to classify papers as method vs non-method or discovery vs non-discovery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small (2018) found 'using' was a very strong predictor for method papers (accuracy 89.5%), and combinations (using + may + consensus + not + show + suggest) achieved ≈92% accuracy. Use logistic regression or similar models and test variable combinations; beware of confounders like publication age and domain.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation scheme design and mapping (polarity <-> function)
rubrics_metrics.description: Design annotation schemes that map functions to polarities and possibly to influence labels; add granular aspects (e.g., comparison: positive/negative/neutral) to improve precision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hernández-Alvarez et al. added aspects to functions (e.g., comparison results positive/negative/neutral) and mapped polarity to function to improve indices of influence. When creating schemes, document mappings, edge cases (multiple functions per citation), and support multi-label annotations because citations can serve multiple functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classifier evaluation considerations (accuracy, precision, class imbalance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Evaluate citation-function/polarity/influence classifiers with appropriate metrics and report class imbalances and per-class performance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reported accuracies vary (function 67–90%, polarity 83–93%, influence up to 94% in some controlled studies). Many functions/purposes are imbalanced (some categories rare), which harms classifier performance (Li et al.). Report precision/recall per class, confusion matrices, and consider sampling or class-weighting strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Citer motivation taxonomies and social/ rhetorical functions
rubrics_metrics.description: Categorize why authors cite (motivation surveys/taxonomies): position, signposting, acknowledging knowing/trustworthy/classical works, argumentation, social alignment, mercantile alignment, data, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Empirical surveys (e.g., Thornley et al., Milard, Erikson & Erlandson) find varied motivations: 'position' and 'signposting' frequent in some fields; 'knowing the cited authors' or citing canonical/seminal works also common. Use such taxonomies to interpret citation functions beyond linguistic signals, and be aware that purely social references are sometimes rare. Allow multi-motive labels where citations serve multiple social/rhetorical purposes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset and domain considerations (corpus selection and generalizability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choice of corpora (ACL Anthology, PubMed, PLOS, IEEE, discipline-specific samples) affects labels, feature distributions, and classifier transferability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies report domain effects (e.g., verb distributions, frequency of 'use' in method papers). Dataset sizes varied widely (from tens to tens of thousands of papers). Class imbalance, domain-specific vocabulary, and sectioning conventions influence performance; validate across domains or report domain-specific limits.
